text: To err on the side of caution
Following our review of the accounts, we recommend a reduction in the price.
The seller's failure to disclose the claim raises a serious question.
Board approval is contingent on the completion of the audit.
The likelihood of resistance from the seller is high.
We went through the accounts, and we think the price has to come down.
They did not tell us about the claim, and that worries me.
Our exposure on the claim is approximately four million dollars.
The bottom line is that the deal still works, but not at this price.

When a junior lawyer sends me a memo, I look for one thing in the first paragraph, and that is the recommendation. If I have to reach page two to find out what you want me to do, the memo has already failed. Written English for a board is built out of nouns: the acquisition, the review, the recommendation, the reduction in price. That is not decoration. A noun lets you pack a whole event into two words and put it at the front of the sentence, where the reader can find it. But the same density that works on the page fails out loud. If you stand up in a meeting and say, following the completion of our review, our recommendation is a reduction in the price, people stop listening by the fourth noun. So when you present the memo, turn the nouns back into verbs. We reviewed the accounts. We found a claim. We think the price should come down. Same content, half the effort for the people in the room.

I have read hundreds of memos in my career, and I remember about three of them. The one I remember best was two pages long. The first line said: we recommend going ahead, subject to three conditions. By the end of the first page I knew the price, the risk, and what it would cost to protect ourselves. The seller hated the escrow. They threatened to walk away twice, and our own sales director wanted to give in. In the end they accepted three million in escrow instead of four, and we closed in May instead of March. Eighteen months later, the tax claim was settled for almost exactly that amount. If that memo had been ten pages of background, I would have signed in March, and the claim would have been our problem instead of theirs.

First, the legal team reviews the target company's documents, including its correspondence with the tax authority. In that correspondence, an unresolved tax claim against the subsidiary comes to light, and it is nowhere in the seller's disclosure. The lawyers then write a two-page memo, with the recommendation in the very first line. The board approves new terms: a lower price, money held in escrow, and a specific indemnity. Finally, after two weeks of resistance, the seller accepts, and the closing date moves from March to May.
